chapter: Cotton Club and radio fame with Cab
title: Recording 'Minnie the Moocher' with Victor Young
summary: The Cotton Club moves downtown; Thomas recalls the session where his strip-paper arrangement was slowed down on Victor Young's suggestion that a minor sounds better slow.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: They opened on 48th and Broadway in 1936.
We opened during the... Now, that's the greatest thing. We opened during the time of the World's Fair...
What did you want to go back to say about what, Foots?

I told you that Cab told me to do something with "Minnie The Moocher" the night we closed at the Cotton Club. We were recording the next day. So I got up the next morning and did my little thing... [SINGS 'GET HAPPY' REFRAIN, 16 BARS] So we got down there the next day and we did all the... See, in those olden days, you had to do four tunes to have a date. So we did the other three tunes, and then they saved "Minnie The Moocher" for the last. So we started out with this arrangement we didn't like, and there was a whole lot of notes jumbled up. So after about three or four times we tried it, Cab said, "Foots, did you do something on "Minnie The Moocher?" I said, "Yes." So I

went to my saxophone case -- and I'd done my arrangement on strips of paper. Wasn't no need to waste no whole sheet of paper on that little introduction. Because when I made the introduction, I said to myself I'd use the same thing for the ending. So I got out the strips of paper and passed them out. I guess I looked foolish passing out strips of paper. All I had on there was that eight bars.

So we got to play my little thing on "Minnie The Moocher," and we was playin' it up-tempo. [SINGS REFRAIN] We did that a couple of times, we still didn't hear it. But the most miraculous thing on the date was who the A&R man was.

He was the genius. We didn't know it then. But I noticed one thing about him. If the first, second or third saxophone squeaked, he could tell which one squeaked. And he'd stop a thing in the middle, because that squeak wasn't going to go in a good recording. His name was Victor Young.

Now, we knew he was a smart little young cat. We didn't find out nothin' about him until later on, when he started writing all them hits. But he was the one... I give him as much credit as anybody else, because at the time that

"Minnie The Moocher" up in the up-tempo, he said, "You know, a minor sounds better slow than it does fast." It made some sense. And Milt, soon as we slowed it up, we all knew we had it. When we said, "Dah-de-dah, da-da, da-da" [ETC.] It just put a new shine on the whole thing. And the funny thing about it, Cab could do the Hi-De-Ho's better, because he was having trouble doing the Hi-De-Ho's fast. And we could the answering better. Everything...

And I don't know how I figured out that we didn't need to playing nothing while he was singing "Minnie The Moocher." All we had to do was sit there and wait and do the answer. Because this other thing had the music all through there, wasn't meaning nothing, wasn't no sense of (?).

And I..I get upset sometimes, but I'm thankful that I learned to know so much about music. Because when Harold Arlen started writing for the Cotton Club, man, he made such a big impression on me. You know, Harold Arlen was a piano player with a band from Buffalo. And he had that... I don't know how to say it. He had that talent that Black musicians have. He had that Blues thing. Because that's how... It was amazing...
